cards.q: What is a nucleophile?
cards.a: An electron pair donor: a species with a lone pair that it uses to form a new covalent bond to an electron-deficient (δ+) atom.
cards.why: Examples: \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\). “Nucleophile” means “nucleus-loving”: it seeks positive charge.

cards.q: Why is the carbon–halogen bond in a halogenoalkane polar, and what does this mean for its reactions?
cards.a: The halogen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbon is \(\delta+\) and the halogen \(\delta-\). The \(\delta+\) carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of bromoethane. The carbon bonded to bromine is labelled δ+ and the bromine δ−, showing the polar C–Br bond.

cards.why: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are all more electronegative than carbon, although the difference falls down the group.

cards.q: How are halogenoalkanes classified as primary, secondary or tertiary?
cards.a: By the number of carbon atoms bonded to the carbon that carries the halogen: one (primary), two (secondary) or three (tertiary).
cards.why: Chloromethane, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}Cl}\), with no other carbon, is usually counted with the primary halogenoalkanes.

cards.q: Name this halogenoalkane and classify it as primary, secondary or tertiary.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula: a central carbon bonded to three methyl groups and a bromine atom.

cards.a: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane: a tertiary halogenoalkane.
cards.why: The carbon bonded to the bromine is also bonded to three other carbons.

cards.q: Name this compound and say whether it is a primary, secondary or tertiary halogenoalkane.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula: a four-carbon chain with a chlorine atom on the second carbon.

cards.a: 2-chlorobutane: a secondary halogenoalkane.
cards.why: The chlorine is on carbon 2, which is bonded to two other carbons. Number from the end that gives the halogen the lowest number.

cards.q: True or false: this compound is branched, so it must be a secondary or tertiary halogenoalkane.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula: a three-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the middle carbon and an iodine atom on an end carbon.

cards.a: False. It is 1-iodo-2-methylpropane, a primary halogenoalkane.
cards.why: Only the carbon carrying the halogen matters: here it is bonded to just one other carbon, wherever the branch is.

cards.q: Give three uses of halogenoalkanes, and say why the use of some has been restricted.
cards.a: Refrigerants, solvents and pharmaceuticals. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were restricted because they damage the ozone layer.
cards.why: Halogenoalkanes are much more reactive than alkanes, which makes them useful starting materials too.

cards.q: Give the reagent and conditions to convert a halogenoalkane into an alcohol.
cards.a: Aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide, warmed or heated under reflux.
cards.why: In water, \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) acts as a nucleophile and substitution happens. In ethanol, elimination takes over.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of bromoethane with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br + NaOH \rightarrow  CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + NaBr}\)

answerFigure.alt: Bromoethane reacts with hydroxide ions, from aqueous sodium hydroxide heated under reflux, to give ethanol and a bromide ion.

cards.why: Ionic form: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br + OH^{-} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}OH + Br^{-}}\). Sodium is a spectator ion.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of bromoethane with hydroxide ions.
cards.a: Nucleophilic substitution.

answerFigure.alt: Nucleophilic substitution: a lone pair on the hydroxide ion attacks the δ+ carbon of bromoethane, and the C–Br bond breaks with both electrons going to bromine, giving ethanol and a bromide ion.

marks: A curly arrow from a lone pair on the O of \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) to the \(\delta+\) carbon.
A curly arrow from the C–Br bond to the Br atom: the bond breaks heterolytically.
Products ethanol and \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\); \(\delta+\)/\(\delta-\) shown on the C–Br bond.

cards.q: In this mechanism, what does each curly arrow show?

figure.alt: Nucleophilic substitution: a lone pair on the hydroxide ion attacks the δ+ carbon of 1-chloropropane, and the C–Cl bond breaks heterolytically, giving propan-1-ol and a chloride ion.

cards.a: The first arrow: the hydroxide ion’s lone pair forming a new bond to the δ+ carbon. The second: the pair of electrons in the C–Cl bond moving onto the chlorine, which leaves as a chloride ion.
cards.why: A curly arrow always shows the movement of a pair of electrons, from where they are to where they end up.

cards.q: True or false: in the mechanism with \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), the curly arrow should start from the minus sign of the hydroxide ion.
cards.a: False. It must start from a lone pair on the oxygen atom.
cards.why: Curly arrows start at a lone pair or a bond: a real pair of electrons. Examiners do not credit an arrow from a charge.

cards.q: Why is the reaction between a halogenoalkane and hydroxide ions called nucleophilic substitution?
cards.a: The attacking species is a nucleophile, and it replaces (substitutes for) the halogen atom.
cards.why: The halogen leaves as a halide ion.

cards.q: Give the reagent and conditions to convert a halogenoalkane into a nitrile.
cards.a: Potassium cyanide dissolved in ethanol (with a little water), heated under reflux.

answerFigure.alt: Bromoethane is heated under reflux with potassium cyanide in ethanol to give propanenitrile, CH3CH2CN; the bromine leaves as bromide.

cards.why: The cyanide ion, \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\), is the nucleophile. Potassium cyanide is highly toxic.

cards.q: Write an ionic equation for the reaction of bromoethane with cyanide ions, and name the organic product.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br + CN^{-} \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CN + Br^{-}}\)
The product is propanenitrile.
cards.why: The carbon of the CN group counts in the name: two carbons from bromoethane plus one from cyanide makes propanenitrile.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the reaction of bromoethane with cyanide ions.
cards.a: Nucleophilic substitution, with the lone pair on the carbon of the cyanide ion attacking.

answerFigure.alt: Nucleophilic substitution: the lone pair on the carbon of the cyanide ion attacks the δ+ carbon of bromoethane, and the C–Br bond breaks, giving propanenitrile and a bromide ion.

marks: A curly arrow from the lone pair on the carbon of \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\) to the \(\delta+\) carbon.
A curly arrow from the C–Br bond to the Br atom.
Products: propanenitrile, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}CN}\), and \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\).

cards.q: Why is the reaction of halogenoalkanes with cyanide ions useful in synthesis?
cards.a: It increases the length of the carbon chain by one carbon atom.
cards.why: The new carbon comes from the cyanide ion. The nitrile can then be converted into other compounds, such as amines or carboxylic acids.

cards.q: True or false: 1-chloropropane reacts with potassium cyanide to give propanenitrile.
cards.a: False. The product is butanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CH₂CN.
cards.why: Three carbons from the chain plus the carbon of the cyanide group make four, so the name is based on butane.

cards.q: Calculate the percentage atom economy for making propanenitrile: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br + KCN \rightarrow CH_{3}CH_{2}CN + KBr}\). Use \(A_{\text{r}}\): H 1.0, C 12.0, N 14.0, K 39.1, Br 79.9.
cards.a: 31.6%
cards.why: Substitution always wastes the atoms of the leaving group and its counter-ion, here as potassium bromide.

cards.q: Give the reagent and conditions to convert a halogenoalkane into a primary amine.
cards.a: Excess concentrated ammonia in ethanol, heated in a sealed tube (under pressure).
cards.why: Ammonia is a gas, so a sealed tube stops it escaping when heated.

cards.q: Write an equation for the reaction of bromoethane with excess ammonia.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}Br + 2NH_{3} \rightarrow  CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2} + NH_{4}Br}\)
cards.why: The second ammonia molecule removes \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from the ethylammonium ion, forming ammonium bromide.

cards.q: Outline the first step of the mechanism for the reaction of bromoethane with ammonia.
cards.a: Nucleophilic substitution: ammonia attacks, giving the ethylammonium ion, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{3}^{+}}\), and \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\).

answerFigure.alt: First step with ammonia: the lone pair on the nitrogen of ammonia attacks the δ+ carbon of bromoethane and the C–Br bond breaks, giving the ethylammonium ion and a bromide ion.

marks: A curly arrow from the lone pair on the N of \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) to the \(\delta+\) carbon.
A curly arrow from the C–Br bond to the Br atom.
The product carries a positive charge on nitrogen: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{3}^{+}}\).

cards.q: Outline the second step of the mechanism for the reaction of bromoethane with ammonia, in which ethylamine forms.
cards.a: A second ammonia molecule acts as a base and removes \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) from the ethylammonium ion.

answerFigure.alt: Second step with ammonia: a lone pair on a second ammonia molecule attacks a hydrogen on the N⁺ of the ethylammonium ion, and the N–H bond breaks with its electrons going to nitrogen, giving ethylamine and an ammonium ion.

marks: A curly arrow from the lone pair on the N of a second \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\) to an H on the \(\mathrm{N^{+}}\).
A curly arrow from that N–H bond to the N atom.
Products: ethylamine, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\), and \(\mathrm{NH_{4}^{+}}\).

cards.q: Explain why excess ammonia is used when making a primary amine from a halogenoalkane.
cards.a: To make further substitution unlikely, so the primary amine is the main product.
marks: The primary amine product also has a lone pair on nitrogen, so it is also a nucleophile.
It can attack more halogenoalkane, giving secondary and tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt.
With ammonia in excess, a halogenoalkane molecule is far more likely to meet ammonia than the amine.

cards.q: Write equations for the hydrolysis of a bromoalkane, RBr, by water, and for the test that follows with silver nitrate.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{RBr + H_{2}O \rightarrow ROH + H^{+} + Br^{-}}\)
\(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq) + Br^{-}(aq) \rightarrow AgBr(s)}\)
cards.why: Water is a weak nucleophile, so this is slow enough to time. The precipitate appears as the halide ions are released.

cards.q: Describe how to compare the rates of hydrolysis of 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane.
cards.a: Put the same volume of ethanol and of aqueous silver nitrate in three test tubes in a water bath at the same temperature. Add the same number of drops of each halogenoalkane, start a timer, and time how long a precipitate takes to appear.
cards.why: A shorter time means a faster hydrolysis. Keeping the carbon chain the same means only the halogen changes.

cards.q: Why is ethanol added when halogenoalkanes are hydrolysed with aqueous silver nitrate?
cards.a: Halogenoalkanes do not dissolve in water. Ethanol is a solvent for both the halogenoalkane and the aqueous silver nitrate, so they mix and react.
cards.why: Without ethanol, the halogenoalkane would form a separate layer and react only at the boundary.

cards.q: What are the precipitates seen when chloro-, bromo- and iodoalkanes are hydrolysed with silver nitrate in ethanol, and which appears first?
cards.a: Chloro: white (AgCl). Bromo: cream (AgBr). Iodo: yellow (AgI). The yellow precipitate from the iodoalkane appears first.
cards.why: The order of appearance shows the order of reactivity: iodo > bromo > chloro.

cards.q: Explain why iodoalkanes are hydrolysed faster than chloroalkanes.
cards.a: The rate depends on how easily the carbon–halogen bond breaks.
marks: The C–I bond has a lower bond enthalpy than the C–Cl bond (C–I is the weakest; C–F the strongest).
Less energy is needed to break C–I, so the activation energy is lower.
So the iodoalkane reacts fastest, even though the C–I bond is the least polar.

cards.q: True or false: the C–Cl bond is the most polar of C–Cl, C–Br and C–I, so chloroalkanes are hydrolysed fastest.
cards.a: False. Chloroalkanes are hydrolysed slowest.
cards.why: Bond enthalpy, not polarity, controls the rate: the strong C–Cl bond is the hardest to break.

cards.q: Why are fluoroalkanes hardly hydrolysed at all, although the C–F bond is very polar?
cards.a: The C–F bond has a very high bond enthalpy, so it is very hard to break.
cards.why: This strength is also why fluorinated compounds are so unreactive and long-lasting.

cards.q: State the order of the rates of hydrolysis of primary, secondary and tertiary halogenoalkanes.
cards.a: Tertiary > secondary > primary: the tertiary halogenoalkane forms a precipitate fastest with silver nitrate in ethanol.
cards.why: To compare fairly, use isomers with the same halogen, such as 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

cards.q: In comparing rates of hydrolysis with silver nitrate, why is the test done with water as the nucleophile, not with sodium hydroxide?
cards.a: Hydroxide ions would react with silver ions to form a precipitate of silver oxide, hiding the silver halide precipitate.
cards.why: Water is also a slower nucleophile, so the times are long enough to measure.

cards.q: Give the reagent and conditions to convert a halogenoalkane into an alkene.
cards.a: Potassium hydroxide dissolved in ethanol, heated under reflux.
cards.why: Here \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) acts as a base, removing \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), and HBr (as water and bromide) is eliminated.

cards.q: Explain how \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) acts as a nucleophile in one reaction of a halogenoalkane and as a base in another.
cards.a: As a nucleophile (substitution) it donates a lone pair to the \(\delta+\) carbon. As a base (elimination) it accepts a proton, \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), from the carbon next to the C–X carbon.
cards.why: Both happen at the same time; the conditions decide which one dominates.

cards.q: Outline the mechanism for the elimination reaction of 2-bromopropane with hydroxide ions.
cards.a: Elimination: the hydroxide ion acts as a base.

answerFigure.alt: Elimination from 2-bromopropane: a lone pair on the hydroxide ion attacks a hydrogen on the carbon next to the C–Br carbon; the C–H bond electrons move to form the C=C bond, and the C–Br bond breaks to give a bromide ion. Products: propene, water and bromide.

marks: A curly arrow from a lone pair on the O of \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) to an H on a carbon next to the C–Br carbon.
A curly arrow from that C–H bond to between the two carbons, forming the C=C bond.
A curly arrow from the C–Br bond to the Br atom; products propene, \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) and \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\).

cards.q: When 2-bromopropane reacts with potassium hydroxide, two organic products can form. Name them and say what type of reaction gives each.
cards.a: Propan-2-ol by nucleophilic substitution, and propene by elimination.

answerFigure.alt: 2-Bromopropane reacts with hydroxide ions in hot ethanolic potassium hydroxide to give propene, water and a bromide ion.

cards.why: Substitution and elimination happen together (concurrently); the conditions decide which product is the main one.

cards.q: Explain which conditions favour substitution and which favour elimination when a halogenoalkane reacts with hydroxide ions.
cards.a: Aqueous and warm favours substitution; ethanolic and hot favours elimination.
marks: Substitution (alcohol) is favoured by an aqueous solvent and a lower temperature.
Elimination (alkene) is favoured by ethanol as the solvent and a higher temperature.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes give more elimination than primary ones.

cards.q: Elimination of HBr from 2-bromobutane gives three different alkenes. Name them.
cards.a: But-1-ene, E-but-2-ene and Z-but-2-ene.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of three alkenes: but-1-ene (double bond at the end of the chain), E-but-2-ene (the two end carbons on opposite sides of the central double bond) and Z-but-2-ene (the two end carbons on the same side).

cards.why: The H can be lost from carbon 1 (giving but-1-ene) or carbon 3 (giving but-2-ene, which has E and Z isomers).

cards.q: True or false: elimination from 1-bromopropane and from 2-bromopropane gives two different alkenes.
cards.a: False. Both give propene.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of propene: a three-carbon chain with a double bond between carbons 1 and 2.

cards.why: Either way, the double bond forms between carbons 1 and 2 of a three-carbon chain; only the substitution products (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol) differ.

cards.q: What do the labels SN1 and SN2 mean?
cards.a: S: substitution. N: nucleophilic. The number is how many species take part in the rate-determining step: one (SN1) or two (SN2).
cards.why: So the rate equation is first order overall for SN1 and second order overall for SN2.

cards.q: The hydrolysis of 1-bromobutane by \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) has rate \(= k[\mathrm{C_{4}H_{9}Br}][\mathrm{OH^{-}}]\). What does this show about the mechanism?
cards.a: It is \(\mathrm{S_{N}2}\): both the halogenoalkane and the hydroxide ion are in the rate-determining step, a single step in which the C–O bond forms as the C–Br bond breaks.
cards.why: Primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2.

cards.q: The hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane has rate \(= k[\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{3}CBr}]\). Outline the mechanism this suggests.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{S_{N}1}\), in two steps.

answerFigure.alt: SN1 hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane. Step 1 (slow): the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically to give a planar tertiary carbocation and a bromide ion. Step 2 (fast): a lone pair on a hydroxide ion attacks the carbocation, giving 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

marks: Only the halogenoalkane is in the rate-determining step, so the slow step is the C–Br bond breaking alone.
Step 1 (slow): heterolytic fission gives a tertiary carbocation, \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{3}C^{+}}\), and \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\).
Step 2 (fast): \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) attacks the carbocation, giving 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

cards.q: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes react by SN1 but primary halogenoalkanes react by SN2.
cards.a: Tertiary carbocations are stable enough to form, and the three alkyl groups block attack; primary are the reverse.
marks: A tertiary carbocation is stabilised by three alkyl groups, which push electron density towards the positive carbon.
In a tertiary halogenoalkane, the three bulky alkyl groups get in the way of a nucleophile attacking the carbon (steric hindrance).
A primary carbocation is too unstable to form, and the carbon is open to attack, so a one-step SN2 reaction happens.

cards.q: A single optical isomer of a halogenoalkane is hydrolysed. How does the optical activity of the product show whether the mechanism was SN1 or SN2?
cards.a: Optically active product: SN2. Racemic mixture with no optical activity: SN1.

answerFigure.alt: SN2 on one optical isomer of 2-bromobutane: hydroxide attacks from the side opposite the bromine, so butan-2-ol forms with its groups inverted, like an umbrella blown inside out.

marks: In SN2, the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the halogen, inverting the arrangement, so a single optical isomer forms: the product rotates plane-polarised light.
In SN1, the carbocation is planar, so the nucleophile attacks from either side with equal probability.
This gives equal amounts of both optical isomers (a racemic mixture), which does not rotate plane-polarised light.

cards.q: Why is ozone in the upper atmosphere beneficial?
cards.a: It absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.
cards.why: Less UV reaches the surface: too much UV causes sunburn, skin cancer and eye damage (cataracts).

cards.q: Name this chlorofluorocarbon (CFC), once used in refrigerators and aerosols.

figure.alt: Displayed formula of a CFC: one carbon atom bonded to two chlorine atoms and two fluorine atoms.

cards.a: Dichlorodifluoromethane, \(\mathrm{CCl_{2}F_{2}}\).
cards.why: Substituents are listed alphabetically: chloro before fluoro.

cards.q: Explain how chlorine atoms form in the upper atmosphere from CFCs.
cards.a: Ultraviolet radiation breaks the C–Cl bonds homolytically.

answerFigure.alt: Ultraviolet light breaks a C–Cl bond in dichlorodifluoromethane homolytically, shown by two fish-hook arrows, one electron going to each atom. Products: the CClF2 radical and a chlorine atom (radical).

marks: CFCs are unreactive, so they last long enough to reach the upper atmosphere.
There, UV radiation has enough energy to break a C–Cl bond.
The bond breaks homolytically, one electron to each atom, releasing a chlorine radical, \(\mathrm{Cl\cdot}\).

cards.q: Why is it the C–Cl bond in a CFC that UV radiation breaks, not the C–F bond?
cards.a: The C–Cl bond is weaker (lower bond enthalpy) than the C–F bond.
cards.why: Fluorine atoms are therefore not released; the C–F bond is one of the strongest single bonds.

cards.q: Write the two equations that show how chlorine atoms catalyse the decomposition of ozone.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Cl\cdot + O_{3} \rightarrow ClO\cdot + O_{2}}\)
\(\mathrm{ClO\cdot + O_{3} \rightarrow 2O_{2} + Cl\cdot}\)
cards.why: Adding them gives the overall equation \(\mathrm{2O_{3} \rightarrow 3O_{2}}\).

cards.q: Explain how the equations for ozone decomposition show that chlorine atoms act as a catalyst.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cl\cdot}\) is used in the first step and made again in the second.
marks: \(\mathrm{Cl\cdot}\) reacts with ozone in the first step and is regenerated in the second.
It does not appear in the overall equation, \(\mathrm{2O_{3} \rightarrow 3O_{2}}\).
So one chlorine atom can destroy many thousands of ozone molecules.

cards.q: How did the scientific community’s work on CFCs lead to change?
cards.a: Research by different groups gave evidence that CFCs deplete ozone, which led to legislation banning CFCs as solvents and refrigerants. Chemists developed chlorine-free alternatives, such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs).
cards.why: HFCs contain no C–Cl bonds, so they release no chlorine atoms.

cards.q: True or false: in \(\mathrm{ClO\cdot + O_{3} \rightarrow 2O_{2} + Cl\cdot}\), the \(\mathrm{ClO\cdot}\) species is a stable molecule, not a radical.
cards.a: False. ClO• is a radical: it has an unpaired electron.
cards.why: Each step in the cycle is a propagation step: a radical reacts and a radical forms, so the chain continues.

cards.q: True or false: the hole in the ozone layer is caused mainly by carbon dioxide.
cards.a: False. It is caused mainly by chlorine atoms from CFCs.
cards.why: Carbon dioxide is linked to global warming, a different problem: it absorbs infrared radiation, not UV.
